summary:
Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory where local legislation governs. United Kingdom law, including the Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex services code, does not extend automatically and could be applied only by Order in Council.

Bermuda has no legal recognition of transgender people. The Human Rights Act has prohibited discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2013, when the Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act, which also banned age discrimination; gender identity is not covered, leaving trans people without statutory protection against discrimination. The sources identify no transgender-specific provisions on documents, screening, facilities, custody, healthcare, penalties or protection machinery.

Expression of gender identity is described as often difficult. In 2006 the Government attempted to bar Mark Anderson, the drag performer known as "Queen of Bermuda" Sybil, from a parade, stating that he contradicted local mores and sensitivities.

Consensual sex between adult men is legal. The House of Assembly voted 22–16 on 14 May 1994 to decriminalise it, striking two sections of the Criminal Code; the debate divided the island, with religious leaders split and the Christian Coalition staging marches against the change. Prior liability carried up to ten years' imprisonment for anal and oral sex. Lesbian activity has never been illegal, and the gross indecency provision between men was repealed in 2019.

The age of consent is unequal: 18 for consensual anal intercourse under the law effective 1 November 2019, against 16 for other sexual activity. A prior higher age of 18 for gay male conduct had been found in violation of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Same-sex marriage is not legally available as of 2022. The Supreme Court legalised it in May 2017 in the Godwin and DeRoche case under the Marriage Act 1944 and the Human Rights Act. The Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act on 7 February 2018, effective 1 June 2018, replacing marriage with domestic partnerships open to same-sex and opposite-sex couples and making Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality. The Supreme Court restored marriage on 6 June 2018 and the Court of Appeal on 23 November 2018, but the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council banned it again on 14 March 2022, with July 2022 laws retrospectively backdating prior legality. Recognition of a partner therefore rests on the partnership register.
tangentialFactors:
Organised religious hostility toward visible same-sex couples is documented: in July the AME church and other Bermuda churches protested a gay cruise as "incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre".

Enforcement of morality-based law has drawn official resources. In November 2020 reporting, the government spent approximately £150,000 to appeal the case of a man charged and threatened with jail under the "obscene behaviour law" for importing gay porn DVDs, a case held unconstitutional.

Bermuda's discrimination protection covers sexual orientation but not gender identity, so a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship falls outside the statutory protection that applies to the relationship's sexual-orientation dimension.
localsOnly:
The Bermuda Regiment, raised by random lottery conscription, officially prohibits discrimination or harassment of LGBT soldiers, though such conduct has been reported as tolerated by officers to the extent that one conscript described the Regiment as "the most homophobic environment that exists".

Gay and bisexual men may donate blood through the Bermuda Hospitals Board if they have not had sex with another man in the past 12 months; a 12-month deferral likewise applies to women who have sex with men who have sex with men.

Same-sex couples may adopt on equal terms under the Adoption of Children Act following the February 2015 Supreme Court ruling on marital-status and sexual-orientation discrimination, and binational same-sex partners were granted equal employment and benefits by the Supreme Court in November 2015.
outOfScopeNotes:
No transgender-specific provisions on documents, screening, facilities, custody, healthcare, enforcement, penalties or protection machinery were identified in the sources. How a trans visitor would be handled at entry, in custody or in medical settings is not sourced.

Whether the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 or its 2025 single-sex services code will be extended to Bermuda by Order in Council is unresolved.

The sources do not record whether the Human Rights Act's omission of gender identity has been tested in any Bermuda court.
